verdict.reasoning: Patient states he woke up about an hour ago and could not move his left arm: "I woke up this morning about an hour ago and I couldn't move my left arm anymore."
He reports no pain and persistent inability to move the arm: "I feel no pain, but just can't move it" and later "The arm still can't move."
Patient notes left facial tingling beginning with symptom onset: "I feel a bit of tingling on the left side of my face" and "So an hour ago."

He describes dribbling when drinking and associated swallowing difficulty: "I was trying to drink earlier and I dribbled a bit" and doctor clarifies "you had some difficulty swallowing, is that right?" Patient: "Yeah."
Speech difficulty is described: "it's more complicated. Maybe be more slow. I need to think more about it."
He denies leg involvement: Doctor: "Have you had any symptoms in your left leg at all?" Patient: "No."

He denies discoloration and coldness: Doctor: "Is there any discoloration in your hand?" Patient: "No." Doctor: "Does your hand feel cold?" Patient: "Not really. The arm feels fine apart from me not be able to move it."
He reports no prior similar episodes: Doctor: "Has this ever happened before?" Patient: "No, no, it's really the first time."
He states sleep was as usual: Doctor: "did you sleep anything in an awkward position or in a different bed... last night?" Patient: "No, Everything as usual."
Past history includes type 2 diabetes: Patient: "I have type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure."
He also reports high blood pressure (hypertension): "I have type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure."
Medication list includes metformin: Patient: "I'm taking metformin, losartan, and amlodipine."
Medication list includes losartan: "I'm taking metformin, losartan, and amlodipine."
Medication list includes amlodipine: "I'm taking metformin, losartan, and amlodipine."
He reports penicillin allergy: Doctor: "Do you have any allergies to any medication?" Patient: "Only penicillin, I believe."
Family history: "My dad has got heart disease, but I don't know. More detail."
Living situation: Doctor: "And are you normally living alone?" Patient: "Yes."
Smoking history: Doctor: "Do you smoke at all?" Patient: "I used to." indicating former smoker.
Alcohol use: Patient: "I will have a few drinks over the weekend, maybe a couple more during the week." and specifies "Beers. Like pints."
Doctor notes this is a telephone visit and cannot see the patient: "Now I can't see you, it's this telephone appointment" and no vitals or physical exam are documented.

Clinician suspects stroke based on symptoms and risk factors: "I'm concerned that some of the symptoms you've got may be some symptoms of a stroke" plus sudden left arm paralysis, facial tingling, swallowing/speech issues, and history of type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure all described earlier.

An ambulance to ED is arranged: "I'm going to arrange one of my colleagues next to me to call an ambulance to your home address now" and later "they'll probably take you down to the local hospital, a e."

Door access instructions: "maybe you could leave the front door unlocked to sit in the hallway" and later "Just make sure that the front door is open. Sit in the hallway by the front door so that they've got access."

Clinician plans to stay on the phone: "what I'm going to do is I'm going to stay on the line until they reach there Just to make sure that you're okay" and "I'm just going to stay on the line, and we'll wait until the ambulance comes."

He explains ED will involve stroke doctor for urgent assessment/treatment: "they will ring through for the stroke doctor for. To assess you, to see whether they can give you any kind of treatment for that."
